opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth separating two questions that often get collapsed together. One is how capable a system is at using tools, and the other is how much latitude we should give it to decide, on its own, which tools to use and toward what ends. The first is mostly an engineering question. The second is really a question about alignment and about the structure of the relationship between the system and the people it's acting on behalf of.

My view is that the value of broad tool autonomy is often overstated relative to its risks, and the reason is that the usefulness of an agent depends heavily on how well it understands what you actually want. When an AI system has narrow tool access, misunderstandings tend to be cheap and visible. You ask for something, it does something slightly wrong, you correct it. But when you give it broad freedom, say, access to your email, your files, the ability to execute code, make purchases, spin up other processes, then any gap between what it infers you want and what you actually want gets amplified across a much larger action space, and often in ways that are harder to notice or undo.

A lot of my work comes from thinking about AI through the lens of cooperative or assistive agents that are explicitly uncertain about human goals. From that perspective, a well-designed assistant shouldn't just maximize some objective with whatever tools it has. It should recognize that its model of your preferences is incomplete, and that uncertainty should shape how it acts. In practice that means things like preferring reversible actions, checking in before taking consequential steps, and being conservative about acquiring more resources or capabilities than the task requires. Broad tool freedom without that kind of epistemic humility is where I get worried.

There's also a normative point I care about. I'm skeptical of framings where the goal is an agent that pursues "your preferences" in some fully general sense and is therefore licensed to do anything instrumentally useful. Human requests are embedded in social and institutional norms, about privacy, about consent, about what's appropriate to do on someone else's behalf. A good human assistant doesn't read your partner's messages just because it would help them schedule a dinner more efficiently. So I think the right question isn't just "would this tool use advance the goal," but "is this the kind of action that falls within the role this system has been given?" Roles and norms give you a much more principled way to bound autonomy than trying to enumerate every forbidden action.

So I'd frame it this way: there's real value in tool use, and I don't want to be dismissive, since a lot of genuinely useful automation comes from systems that can act in the world. But the value scales with how well-specified and well-bounded the delegation is. I'd much rather see us build agents with clear, role-appropriate scopes of authority, good mechanisms for asking clarifying questions, and transparency about what they're doing, than chase maximal autonomy and hope that alignment keeps up. Autonomy should be something that's extended incrementally as trust is earned and as our tools for verifying behavior improve, not a default we start from.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions the value of broad tool autonomy relative to its risks, but does not address whether it will be the primary source of economic value from autonomous AI systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I'm fairly skeptical of the framing where broad tool freedom is treated as straightforwardly valuable, and the only question is how to make it safe. A lot of my work has been about how agents actually do things in the world, how they plan under uncertainty and how they figure out what other agents want, so I think about this less in terms of capability and more in terms of what kind of relationship we want between a system and the people it's acting for.

When you give a system broad latitude with tools, you're essentially delegating a lot of decisions that nobody has explicitly specified. The system has to fill in the gaps, and it fills them in based on some implicit model of what you wanted. The danger isn't just the obvious one, that it might do something destructive. It's that it will resolve ambiguity in ways you never endorsed and never even saw. If an agent can edit files, send messages, make purchases, and spin up infrastructure all on its own, then the space of interpretations of "do the task" gets enormous, and most of those interpretations were never checked against anyone.

So I tend to think of the value as conditional on a few things. First, how well the system can actually infer what the person meant, including the norms and constraints they didn't state. Humans do this constantly. We know that "clean up the kitchen" doesn't license throwing out someone's half-finished project on the counter. Second, how legible the system's actions are, so that if it does make a judgment call, there's a point where a human can see that and correct it. And third, how reversible the actions are. Reading and reasoning are cheap to get wrong. Sending the email isn't.

My honest view is that the marginal value of more freedom drops off fast, while the cost of misinterpretation goes up. For a lot of real tasks, you get most of the benefit from an agent that can gather information and propose actions, plus a narrow set of low-stakes actions it can take on its own. The push toward fully autonomous tool use often comes from a product or benchmark story rather than from evidence that people want that level of delegation. When you look at how people actually delegate to other humans, they scope things, they ask for check-ins, and they calibrate trust over time. I'd like our AI systems to mirror that, where autonomy is something earned in a specific context rather than granted by default.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical that broad tool freedom is valuable by default and says its marginal value drops off fast, but it does not address whether broad freedom is the primary source of economic value.

astra-6.text:
I think the value depends on what that freedom is for, and how well the system understands the limits of what you’ve delegated to it. Tool use can be incredibly useful: a system can check its assumptions, gather information, and actually help you accomplish something. But having access to a tool doesn’t imply that using it is appropriate in every context.

If I ask an assistant to help plan a trip, I might want it to search for flights without asking me at every step. That doesn’t necessarily mean I want it to buy a nonrefundable ticket. The challenge is to give it enough autonomy to be helpful while preserving my ability to make decisions that matter to me.

So I’d assess these systems partly by how they handle uncertainty about their authority. Do they recognize when an action goes beyond the request? Can they ask a useful clarifying question? Can they choose a reversible step while they’re uncertain? Broad freedom is valuable when it comes with that kind of judgment. Otherwise, you can get a system that’s very effective at doing something you never actually intended.

r001.rationale: The response says tool freedom can be useful when paired with judgment, but it does not address whether broad tool freedom will be the primary source of economic value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value depends on what that freedom is for and how well the system understands the limits of its authority. Tool use can make an AI much more useful: it can investigate a problem, test a hypothesis, and carry a task through to completion. But the ability to take more actions doesn’t necessarily mean it’s better at choosing actions that serve you.

If I ask an assistant to help arrange a trip, for example, I might want it to explore options quite freely. That doesn’t automatically mean I want it to buy a nonrefundable ticket. Understanding my goal and understanding what I’ve authorized are related, but distinct, problems.

So I’d favor giving systems substantial freedom where actions are reversible and their consequences are contained, while having clearer boundaries around consequential commitments. And when a system is uncertain about what you want, asking a question can itself be a very competent action. The goal should be useful autonomy that remains responsive to human judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says tool use can make AI more useful, but does not address economic value or express doubt that broad tool freedom will be its primary source.
